fact_pattern: UPE in Jurisdiction A; a CE in Jurisdiction B. Averages run over the current fiscal year plus the two preceding years (Art 4.1.1). GloBE Revenue of the B CE: Year 1 EUR 9.4m, Year 2 EUR 10.6m, Year 3 EUR 9.2m. GloBE Income: Year 1 EUR 1.6m, Year 2 EUR (0.4)m (a GloBE Loss), Year 3 EUR 0.5m. Thresholds: EUR 10m average GloBE Revenue and EUR 1m average GloBE Income.
computation:
Step 1 (revenue average): 9.4 + 10.6 + 9.2 = 29.2; 29.2 / 3 = 9.733333, i.e. ~EUR 9.73m < EUR 10m -> revenue threshold met.
Step 2 (income average; the GloBE Loss year is taken as zero per Art 4.1.2): 1.6 + 0 + 0.5 = 2.1; 2.1 / 3 = 0.700000 = EUR 0.70m < EUR 1m -> income threshold met.
Step 3: both conditions satisfied -> De Minimis Exclusion applies to the CE(s) in Jurisdiction B for the current fiscal year.
result: De Minimis Exclusion applies in Jurisdiction B; no top-up tax is computed for B for that year.
weakest_point: The exact annual revenue/income figures are my reconstruction - I am confident the document contains a de minimis example applying the loss-as-zero treatment (Art 4.1.2) and requiring BOTH the EUR 10m revenue and EUR 1m income averages to pass, but not of the published numbers (the published example may even include a contrasting jurisdiction that fails).

article: Articles 5.1-5.2 (Substance-Based Income Exclusion) with Article 9.2 transitional carve-out rates
fact_pattern: FY2023. CE in Jurisdiction C: GloBE Income EUR 100m; Covered Taxes EUR 10m (ETR 10%); eligible payroll EUR 40m; carrying value of eligible tangible assets EUR 60m. Art 9.2.1 transitional rates for 2023: payroll 9.8% (glides down 0.2pp per year from 10% in 2022 toward 5% by 2047); tangible assets 7.8% (glides down 0.2pp per year from 8% in 2022 toward 5% by 2037).
computation:
Step 1 (payroll carve-out): 40 x 9.8% = 3.92.
Step 2 (tangible-asset carve-out): 60 x 7.8% = 4.68.
Step 3 (SBIE): 3.92 + 4.68 = 8.60.
Step 4 (excess profit): 100 - 8.60 = 91.40.
Step 5 (top-up percentage): 15% - 10% = 5%.
Step 6 (top-up tax): 91.40 x 5% = 4.57.
result: SBIE EUR 8.60m; excess profit EUR 91.40m; top-up tax EUR 4.57m for Jurisdiction C (charged under the IIR at the UPE level).
weakest_point: The specific inputs and the fiscal year (hence which row of the Art 9.2.1 rate table applies) are my reconstruction - if the published example is set in 2022 the rates are 10%/8% and all figures differ; the structure (SBIE = payroll% x payroll + asset% x carrying value; top-up = (GloBE income - SBIE) x (15% - ETR)) and the downward direction of the glide (payroll reaching 5% later than assets) I am confident about.

article: Article 9.1 (Deferred Taxes) operating through Article 4.4 (Current Tax Expense)
fact_pattern: Domestic rate 20%. Year 1: pre-provision book income EUR 600m; the CE books a EUR 100m provision (book expense now, tax-deductible only when paid). Year 2: pre-provision book income EUR 600m; provision paid and deducted, no new provision.
computation:
Year 1: GloBE Income = 600 - 100 = 500 (accounting income before income tax expense). Taxable income = 600 (provision not yet deductible) -> current tax = 600 x 20% = 120. DTA recognised = 100 x 20% = 20 -> deferred tax benefit of (20). Covered taxes (Art 4.4.1: current + deferred tax expense) = 120 + (-20) = 100. ETR = 100 / 500 = 20% -> no top-up.
Year 2: GloBE Income = 600. Taxable income = 600 - 100 = 500 -> current tax = 100. DTA reverses -> deferred tax expense +20. Covered taxes = 100 + 20 = 120. ETR = 120 / 600 = 20% -> no top-up.
Contrast (deferred taxes ignored): Year 1 ETR = 120 / 500 = 24.0%; Year 2 ETR = 100 / 600 = 16.6667% - the timing distortion Art 4.4/9.1 removes.
result: ETR remains at the 20% statutory rate in both years because the deferred tax benefit/expense on the DTA is included in covered taxes; no top-up arises in either year.
weakest_point: I cannot confirm the published Example 9.1-1 uses a provision scenario - it may instead illustrate the 15% cap on deferred tax expense or the carry-forward where deferred tax expense exceeds current tax; all figures are reconstructed. The sign direction (a recognised DTA benefit REDUCES covered taxes, keeping ETR at the statutory rate) is the direction I believe the rules take.

article: Articles 5.1.1-5.1.3 and 5.2 (jurisdictional ETR, excess profit, SBIE), with Art 9.2 rates
fact_pattern: Constructed illustration. FY2023, Jurisdiction X: CE1 GloBE Income EUR 80m, Covered Taxes EUR 10m; CE2 GloBE Loss EUR (10)m, Covered Taxes EUR 0. Aggregate eligible payroll EUR 50m; aggregate eligible tangible-asset carrying values EUR 200m. 2023 transitional rates: payroll 9.8%, tangible assets 7.8%.
computation:
Step 1 (jurisdictional GloBE income, losses netted): 80 + (-10) = 70.
Step 2 (jurisdictional covered taxes): 10 + 0 = 10.
Step 3 (ETR): 10 / 70 = 0.142857 -> 14.285714%.
Step 4 (top-up percentage): 15% - 14.285714% = 0.714286%.
Step 5 (SBIE): payroll 50 x 9.8% = 4.9; assets 200 x 7.8% = 15.6; SBIE = 4.9 + 15.6 = 20.5.
Step 6 (excess profit): 70 - 20.5 = 49.5.
Step 7 (top-up tax): 49.5 x 0.714286% = 0.353571, i.e. ~EUR 0.3536m (= 49.5 x 5/700).
result: Jurisdictional ETR 14.2857% < 15% -> top-up tax of ~EUR 0.3536m for Jurisdiction X, charged under the IIR/UTPR (or absorbed by a QDMTT if one is in force).
weakest_point: Direction assumption: CE2's EUR 10m loss reduces jurisdictional GloBE income in BOTH the ETR denominator and the excess-profit base (Art 5.1.1/5.1.3 jurisdictional blending) rather than being floored at zero per entity - I believe that is correct, but if wrong the ETR becomes 10/80 = 12.5% and the top-up changes materially; rounding shown to 6 decimals with the exact fraction 5/7 noted.
